Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' is inconsistent as written: it is phrased like a trigger ('seeing people...') rather than a strategy the patient uses. Within the Maladaptive Strategies node, the other items are clear coping behaviours, so this item is internally mismatched.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically as a distraction is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as clinically poorly integrated with the rest of the selected items. The other strategies are avoidance/disengagement (screen use, avoiding people), and the threat/memory profile is hypervigilance plus overwhelm. This item introduces a much more extreme coping style without supporting indicators elsewhere in the five target components, making the strategy set feel internally uneven for the same patient.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a police-related trauma in a 46-year-old civilian graphic designer, self-blame for 'the way I acted' is possible, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals that frame the trauma as globally ruining life and draining meaning, without any other items suggesting perceived responsibility, moral failure, or a specific behavior during the event. The appraisal set is therefore less coherent than the other nodes.

vignette: Elias had never considered the night the city's patrol car boxed him in until the tactical lights cut through his studio. He was forty-two, a graphic designer accustomed to quiet hours, when the siren's wail shattered his routine. Two officers had approached with aggressive posture, their hands hovering near their duty belts. When a fleeing suspect stumbled against Elias's porch railing, the encounter escalated into a forceful takedown. Elias watched, paralyzed, as the suspect's jacket tore open, revealing a deep, weeping laceration across his shoulder and a split lip that bled freely onto the concrete. Over the following weeks, the sight of similar wounds on television or on the street would instantly pull him back, forcing the memory of the takedown to resurface with full intensity. Each sudden recall brought such overwhelming emotion that Elias would have to physically stop what he was doing, his breath catching in his throat. When his wife tried to gently ask what was wrong, he would lose the thread of his story, unable to explain clearly how a routine evening had fractured into chaos. His negative appraisals began to color every subsequent experience. He was certain the system had failed to deliver justice, leaving a deep sense of injustice that festered, and he believed nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. This bitter belief warped his perception of everyday encounters, making ordinary police patrols or authority figures feel like immediate provocations rather than background noise. Whenever a patrol car rolled past or a uniformed officer came into view, that direct trigger immediately flooded his nervous system, leaving his body constantly tense and ready to react to danger. His deep sense of injustice and belief that his life was destroyed directly intensified his threat system, ensuring his body remained unable to relax even in the safety of his own bed. His conviction that his world had been destroyed made the trauma feel more immediate, which in turn made the original memories feel more vivid and inescapable. As the memories returned with greater frequency, they directly amplified his hypervigilance, flooding his nervous system before he could escape. To manage the crushing weight of these returning memories, Elias developed habits that slowly isolated him. The intrusive thoughts and sudden flashbacks drove him to spend long hours on his phone, playing games or scrolling through websites to keep his mind occupied. He avoided people, canceling dinner plans with his wife and steering clear of crowded spaces. These maladaptive strategies, initially meant to shield him, soon reinforced his fear network. By constantly distracting himself, he never allowed his brain to process the event, which meant the unprocessed memories only grew sharper and more frequent. His screen escape and mental distraction actually amplified his triggers; the silence left by his avoidance made any sudden noise or sight of authority feel like an invasion. This avoidance also fed his threat system, keeping his body on high alert and preventing him from ever relaxing. Conversely, his escalating threat state-his constant physical tension and exit-planning-made the memories feel more urgent, pulling him further into the cycle. He would catch himself scanning every room for escape routes before sitting down, his anxiety spiking whenever a police cruiser passed, only to retreat to his study and dive back into digital noise, trapping himself in a self-reinforcing loop that left him exhausted and disconnected. At forty-six, Elias sat in his darkened studio, the glow of his monitor reflecting in his tired eyes. His design deadlines piled up, but he found himself staring at blank canvases, his work suffering as his mind fixated on the unfairness of it all. What finally brought him to seek help was the morning he realized he could no longer look at his wife without fearing he would collapse under the weight of his own dread. He hoped for relief from the suffocating tension, but he feared that stepping out of his carefully constructed avoidance would leave him exposed to a world that had already taken everything from him.
